item.title: Change of job for border workers over 55: protections and pension
item.description: When you change position after the age of 55 as a border worker, the tax treatment, occupational pension and the impact on LPP reset. Here are the protections provided by the New 2024 Agreement.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Frontier workers over 55 benefit from specific protections when changing jobs - Tax at source is withheld ONLY in Switzerland; Italy avoids double taxation - From 1 January 2024, the New Frontier Agreement introduces exemption regimes
## Key facts - **What**: Changing jobs as a border worker with tax and pension implications - When: From 1 January 2024 (New Frontier Agreement in force) - Where: Canton of Ticino and Switzerland-Italy border - Who: Frontier workers with G permit, in particular over 55 years of age - AVS/AI/IPG rates: 5.3% (employee) - Exemption: €7,500 (old frontier workers, transitional regime 2024–2033), €10,000 (new frontier workers) - LPP: Varies by age group between 7% and 18% of gross salary
Changing job position after 55 years as a border worker Ticino-Italy presents specific challenges that do not concern Swiss-resident workers. The change of employer is not a simple administrative procedure: it involves readjustments to taxation, occupational security and the sustainability of the pension position in the two States. Since 1 January 2024, with the entry into force of the New Frontier Agreement (signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023), the regulatory landscape has changed significantly, introducing exemptions and transitional regimes that directly affect the border worker who operates a relocation.
The first issue is the tax issue. A ### Implications for occupational security
The second pillar (LPP, Leistungsprivatversicherung) is the crucial node of job change for a border worker over 55. When changing employers in Switzerland, the frontier worker has to deal with the transfer of his pension fund from the previous company to the new one. The employee's contribution varies by age group: from 25 onwards, the percentage varies between 7% and 18% of the gross salary, depending on the age group and the fund. For a worker who changes position, this means renegotiating contribution terms with the new organization.
The biggest risk is the reduction of the contribution rate during transfers. If the previous company paid 16% and the new company offers 14%, the difference affects the accumulated pension amount up to the time of retirement. The redemption value of the LPP must be explicitly requested from the previous fund and transferred to the new one within 30 days of the exchange; failure to redeem means partial loss of contributory years, with consequences on future income.
### Double Taxation and Tax Credit
Although Switzerland does not apply a complementary tax on border workers, Italy maintains the theoretical right of taxation on the worldwide income of the resident. The protection comes from the tax credit: in form 730 of the Italian declaration, the border worker reports the Swiss tax paid and deducts it from the Italian personal income tax due.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Operational procedure: step-by-step job change
Notifying the change of employer to the SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) is the first crucial step: this ensures that the G permit is updated in the system and there are no interruptions in the contribution coverage. The application must be submitted within 8 days of the termination of the previous employment. Simultaneously, the cross-border commuter must communicate the change to the cantonal tax office (AFC/ESTV at the federal level, or the cantonal administration of contributions of Ticino): this is crucial so that the withholding tax rate is updated with the new employer. If not notified, the new employer may apply a standard rate, sometimes higher than the due one, with consequent refunds in the declaration.
The new employer, from the first day of work, must enroll the cross-border commuter in their LPP fund and pay the mandatory contributions. It is advisable to verify, before signing the contract, that the pension fund offers at least the minimum legal contribution. The redemption value of the previous LPP must be requested in writing within 30 days; the transfer occurs directly between the two funds, without passing through the individual.
### Tax declaration: the CE section and refunds
The income tax return remains the critical moment. In the Italian model 730, the CE section (foreign employment income) must accurately report: the gross amount received, the Swiss tax paid, and the amounts of AVS/AI contributions. If the withholding tax rate was incorrect due to failure to communicate the change of employer, it is possible to obtain a refund in the subsequent declaration, a procedure that can take 12-18 months. It is equally important to verify that the new employer has correctly communicated the insurance position to the Swiss information system (UPI): administrative errors at this stage generate gaps in AVS payments, which can only be compensated with lengthy procedures at the INPS.
A cross-border commuter over 55 who changes position at a critical moment in their career should consider consulting with a specialist in cross-border taxation. The margins for administrative error are significant: late communication to the SECO or the Ticino tax office can be costly in unpaid taxes or missed deadlines. Use [nav:calculator] to simulate the tax impact of the new position; [nav:pension] allows you to evaluate how the LPP change will affect your future pension income.

item.title: Border VAT number: self-employed in Switzerland
item.description: Practical guide for border workers who want to start a self-employed business in Switzerland. G permit requirements, taxation, deductibles and social security from 2024.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New Cross-Border Agreement from 1 January 2024: allowances €7,500 (old) or €10,000 (new) - Withholding tax deducted ONLY in Switzerland; Italy recognizes tax credit - Self-employed: AVS 5.3%, AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7-18% by age group - LAMal mandatory; cross-border workers G have the right to choose between Switzerland and Italy
## Key facts - What: Opening a self-employed activity as a cross-border worker in Switzerland - When: From 1 January 2024 (New Cross-Border Agreement in force) - Where: Canton Ticino and Italian-Swiss border - Who: Cross-border workers with a valid Permit G - Amount: Allowance €7,500 (old) or €10,000 (new) - Rate: Withholding tax deducted by Switzerland - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7-18% according to age
Opening a VAT number as a cross-border worker in Switzerland requires understanding cross-border taxation, mandatory social security, and insurance obligations. The New Cross-Border Agreement, which came into force on 1 January 2024, has introduced significant changes for those residing in Italy and working self-employed in Switzerland. The distinction between "old" cross-border workers (already such before 17 July 2023) and "new" affects allowances and tax management directly.
### Self-employed work vs. employed work for cross-border workers
The decision to become self-employed in Switzerland entails administrative and tax responsibilities different from employed work. An employed cross-border worker has the withholding tax deducted directly from the salary by the Swiss employer; a self-employed person, however, must manage the obligations towards the Swiss and Italian authorities autonomously.
In the self-employed work regime in Switzerland, the cross-border worker does not have an "employer" who pays the withholding tax. However, the Convention between Italy and Switzerland of 9 December 1976, integrated by the New Agreement of 23 December 2020 (in force 1 January 2024), establishes that the withholding tax remains deducted exclusively in Switzerland. Italy, to avoid double taxation, recognizes a tax credit (quadro CE of the 730) on those incomes.
### Basic requirements to open a VAT number in Switzerland
For a cross-border worker residing in Italy (Canton Ticino or border provinces) who wants to work self-employed in Switzerland, the following are necessary:
1. Valid Permit G – The cross-border permit allows self-employed work in Switzerland for a maximum duration of five years, renewable. 2. Registration with the cantonal statistical office – Each Swiss canton requires the registration of a self-employed activity with the Cantonal Statistical Office (USTAT, or equivalent body). 3. Swiss federal taxpayer number – Necessary to pay social security contributions (AVS, AI, IPG) and declare income to the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV). 4. Registration with the Italian INPS – To manage the Italian social security position (if applicable for cross-border workers in transitional regime).
The New Cross-Border Agreement distinguishes between old and new cross-border workers regarding the income allowance for self-employed work. Old cross-border workers (already cross-border workers before 17 July 2023) benefit from an annual allowance of €7,500 in the absence of payments received from an employer. New cross-border workers (from 17 July 2023 onwards) enjoy a higher allowance of €10,000. Beyond these amounts, income is subject to the ordinary tax regime. ### Swiss taxation for self-employed border workers
For a border freelancer, Swiss taxation consists of three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. Federal income tax is collected directly from the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV) and is calculated progressively. The Canton of Ticino applies additional cantonal and municipal rates, which vary depending on the municipality in which the activity is carried out.
The central element for the autonomous border crossing is the tax at source. Unlike employee work (where the employer pays the withholding tax on salary), the self-employed person must make quarterly or annual payments. However, Switzerland and Italy have agreed that this tax remains withheld exclusively in Switzerland. Italy recognizes the tax credit in the tax return (EC framework of declaration 730 for border workers who also declare in Italy). It is advisable to use the [calcolatore fiscale](nav:calculator) to simulate the impact of contributions on the net paycheck.
### Italy-Switzerland double taxation agreement
The Convention between Italy and Switzerland, signed on 9 December 1976, provides that income from self-employment carried out in Swiss territory is to be taxed exclusively by Switzerland. This means that:
1. Switzerland taxes the income of the self-employed (tax at source + income tax) 2. Italy DOES NOT tax the same income again 3. The border worker who resides in Italy and earns in Switzerland
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Health insurance (LAMal) and supplementary pension schemes
One of the lesser-known but crucial aspects for the self-employed cross-border worker is health insurance (LAMal, or mandatory basic insurance). Switzerland requires that all residents and workers be enrolled in private health insurance. However, cross-border workers (Permit G) have an option: they can remain enrolled in the Italian insurance system or switch to a Swiss insurance fund.
Many cross-border workers choose to stay in the Italian system (SSN), paying a contribution to the INPS. Those who enroll in Swiss insurance must choose a private fund and pay the monthly premium directly. Swiss deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 depending on the chosen coverage model.
For the third pillar (3a), the self-employed cross-border worker can make voluntary supplementary pension contributions. The annual maximum is defined by Swiss federal legislation and depends on whether the self-employed worker is enrolled in an LPP. Consult the [AVS and LPP guide](nav:pension) to better understand the pension options.
### Practical procedure: step by step
Step 1: Verify cross-border status and register with the competent canton. Request the Permit G from the migration authorities of your Italian province of residence (police headquarters or prefecture). The permit is valid for 5 years.
Step 2: Register with the competent cantonal office. Once you have the Permit G, register your self-employed activity with the cantonal statistical office (USTAT or equivalent). Contact the canton office directly where you will carry out your activity.
Step 3: Obtain the federal taxpayer number and Swiss VAT identification number. The AFC/ESTV will assign a unique federal taxpayer number (UID). If you make VAT transactions, request the UID-VAT number from the same administration.
Step 4: Payment of pension contributions. Register with an AVS compensation organization for the payment of AVS/AI/IPG contributions. For the LPP, a registered cantonal pension fund will proceed with the collection.
Step 5: Health insurance. If you choose to remain in the Italian system, notify your INPS fund of the change in status (from employee to self-employed cross-border worker). If you opt for a Swiss fund, choose a private fund in the canton and enroll directly.
Step 6: Annual tax declaration in Switzerland. By the deadline set by the canton (usually late February or late March of the following year), submit the Swiss tax return to the AFC/ESTV. Attach income and business expense documents.
Step 7: Tax declaration in Italy. Even if self-employed in Switzerland, if you are a resident in Italy, you must declare your Swiss income to the Italian Revenue Agency (model 730 or personal income tax). In the CE section, request the tax credit for taxes paid in Switzerland.
For a personalized simulation of your tax situation, use the [cross-border tax calculator](nav:calculator) available on Frontaliere Ticino. You will immediately receive an estimate of your annual net income and deductions according to your income bracket.

item.title: G-bewilligung: procedure and costs for border workers
item.description: Permit G: CHF 65 cost, 5 years validity. Complete application guide at the Migrationsamt for border workers Ticino-Italy.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- G permit valid for 5 years for cross-border workers in Switzerland - Application cost: 65 CHF at the Migrationsamt - Required documents: identity, employment contract, proof of income - Renewal possible within 12 months before expiration
## Key facts
- **What**: G permit for cross-border workers (Grenzgänger) - When: Valid for 5 years from issuance - Where: Migrationsamt (cantonal immigration office) - Who: Cross-border workers residing in Italy who work in Switzerland - Amount: CHF 65 for the application - Renewal: Possible 12 months before expiration
The G permit is an essential tool for cross-border workers who regularly work in Switzerland. Unlike other forms of work authorization, the permit is specifically designed for those who reside in Italy and cross the border daily to work for Swiss companies in the Canton of Ticino. The application procedure is not complex but requires attention to administrative details. The Migrationsamt, the competent office for immigration, handles all requests for issuance and renewal. With a cost of only 65 CHF, the permit represents a modest investment to ensure a regularized and recognized work position by Swiss authorities.
### What is the G permit and who is eligible
The G permit (Grenzgängerbewilligung) is a form of work authorization specifically intended for cross-border workers who reside permanently in Italy and perform dependent work in Switzerland. Its five-year validity makes it particularly convenient for those intending to maintain long-term employment in the Swiss territory. It is not a residence permit: the G permit allows working in Switzerland while maintaining fiscal and legal residence in Italy. This feature distinguishes it from the B permit (Aufenthaltsbewilligung), which is intended for those who actually move to Switzerland and change their residence. The Permesso G greatly simplifies the administrative life of the cross-border commuter. Those who cross the border daily at Chiasso, Brogeda or other crossings in the Ticino region thus have a document recognized by the Swiss authorities and the tax offices of both countries. One of the most important practical implications concerns taxation: as a cross-border commuter with Permesso G, the withholding tax on employment income is made solely in Switzerland. Italy, for its part, recognizes the tax credit to avoid double taxation. This mechanism is configured in the income tax return 730, in the CE section specifically for cross-border commuters. Differences between Permesso G and Permesso B Many cross-border commuters confuse Permesso G with Permesso B. The distinction is fundamental: Permesso G is for those who reside in Italy and work in Switzerland while maintaining their residence in Italy (cross-border commuter). Permesso B is for those who move and change their residence to Switzerland. For a Ticino-Italy cross-border commuter, Permesso G is almost always the correct choice and offers greater administrative and tax advantages compared to the alternative. Practical scenario: how Permesso G influences the pay slip Suppose a cross-border commuter starts a new job with a company in the Canton of Ticino. Once the Permesso G has been issued by the Migrationsamt, the Swiss employer will apply the AVS/AI/IPG contribution (5.3% for the employee) and the contributions for accident insurance (LAINF, 0.7–1.5% depending on the professional risk). The withholding tax, calculated on a federal and cantonal basis, will not be reported on the pay slip as double taxation: it is already the final tax for the cross-border commuter. Italy, in the 730 declaration, will recognize the Swiss tax credit, thus avoiding the same income being taxed twice.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Practical Procedure: How to Apply for the G Permit
The application for the G Permit is not complicated, but it must follow official channels. Here are the essential steps:
### Step-by-Step Application Procedure
1. Gather Documents — Before presenting yourself at the Migrationsamt, prepare a valid identity document (passport or Italian ID card), a work contract signed by the Swiss employer (copy), proof of income (preliminary pay slips or employer's statement), and the application form provided by the Migrationsamt itself.
2. Submit the Application — Go to the Migrationsamt of the canton where you will work (in this case, Canton Ticino). The application must be submitted on paper or possibly online according to local procedures. The office will guide you on the fastest submission method for your situation.
3. Pay the Fee — The application cost is 65 CHF. This amount is due at the time of application, generally payable directly at the office or through the methods indicated by the Migrationsamt.
4. Processing Time — The Migrationsamt normally processes the application within a few weeks. Once approved, you will receive the G Permit by mail. It is advisable to contact the office to know the specific times in your situation.
### Validity and Renewal
The G Permit is valid for 5 years from issuance. It does not expire suddenly: you have plenty of time to plan the renewal without rush. Renewal can be requested within the 12 months preceding the expiry date. It is advisable to start the renewal procedure at least 2-3 months before the expiry date, to avoid administrative problems or periods without valid authorization. The renewal cost is the same: 65 CHF. Many cross-border workers renew the permit even before the 5 years if the employer or workplace in Switzerland changes.
### Available Tools for the Cross-Border Worker
During the application and permit request process, it is useful to have a tool that helps you understand your tax and contribution obligations. If you want to better understand how the G Permit affects your overall tax situation, a [net calculation tool](nav:calculator) could help you plan your monthly budget and predict the impact of deductions on your Swiss pay slip.
Subscribe to the Frontaliere Ticino newsletter to receive updates on renewal procedures, tax deadlines, and news on cross-border work permits.

## In brief - Third pillar (3a) is a voluntary Swiss supplementary pension fund - Tax deductibility on amounts paid, tax-free returns in Switzerland - Cross-border workers Ticino-Italy can join as Italian residents working in Switzerland - New Agreement 2024: €10,000 exemption for new cross-border workers
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss complementary pension system (third pillar 3a) - When: Accessible to cross-border workers from the New Agreement effective January 1, 2024 - Where: Switzerland, managed by Swiss banks and insurance companies - Who: Employees and self-employed workers, including cross-border workers residing in Italy - Rates: LPP (second pillar) 7-18% by age group; AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% for employees
Swiss pension system is based on three pillars: the first is AVS (old-age and survivors' insurance), the second is LPP (mandatory company pension fund), the third is the voluntary 3a pillar. While the first two are mandatory for those working in Switzerland, the third pillar is optional but offers significant tax advantages, especially for cross-border workers residing in Italy.
The third pillar 3a allows the worker to allocate additional amounts to pension savings, obtaining a deduction from the Swiss taxable income in the same year of payment. For cross-border workers with a G permit working in Switzerland, the mechanism is particularly advantageous: withholding tax on the pay slip is only deducted in Switzerland (never in Italy), as well as the deductibility of the third pillar applies fully to the Swiss taxable base.
### Structure of the three Swiss pillars
The first pillar (AVS/AI/IPG) provides a minimum old-age pension. The second pillar (LPP) is the company pension fund where both the employer and the employee make mandatory contributions: the rate borne by the employee is 5.3% for AVS/AI/IPG, while for the LPP itself the withholding varies from 7% to 18% depending on the worker's age. The third pillar fills the gap between the AVS/LPP pension and the desired salary, ensuring autonomy in personal pension design.
Who can access the third pillar? Cross-border workers residing in Italy who work in Switzerland can join immediately. The only constraint is to have a declared income in Switzerland: a cross-border worker with a G permit who earns the first franc in Switzerland can subscribe to a 3a plan with any Swiss bank or insurance company. The deposit remains locked until retirement (except for exceptions such as purchasing the main residence or starting a business), thus ensuring a long-term reserve.
### Immediate tax advantages
The most immediate advantage is deductibility. Every franc (CHF) paid into the third pillar reduces the Swiss taxable income by the same amount. If a cross-border worker pays CHF 5,000 into 3a in a year, their gross taxable income is reduced by CHF 5,000, resulting in less withholding tax and a lower amount declared to the Swiss tax authorities. In Italy, the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement (effective January 1, 2024) provides a €10,000 exemption for new cross-border workers: this means that amounts paid into the third pillar enjoy additional tax protection in the calculation of double taxation, thanks to the tax credit reported in the CE section of the Italian [tax return](nav:tax-return). ## Application of the New Agreement 2024: Exemption and Refunds
The New Cross-Border Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and effective from January 1, 2024, has introduced specific rules on the taxation of employment income for those residing in Italy and working in Switzerland. One of the novelties concerns the exemption: new cross-border workers (those who started working in Switzerland after July 17, 2023) benefit from an annual exemption of €10,000 on employment income. Cross-border workers already residing before this date, however, enjoy a transitional regime with an exemption of €7,500, valid until 2033.
### How the 3a deductibility interacts with the tax credit
In Italy, cross-border workers declare their gross Swiss income in the 730 form (section 'foreign income'). Since the withholding tax is levied in Switzerland (where the cross-border worker works), the Italian tax authorities apply a tax credit (quadro CE of the declaration) to avoid double taxation. The third pillar comes into play here: the contributions paid reduce the Swiss taxable income, thus reducing the withholding tax paid in Switzerland. This lower Swiss tax is directly reflected in the calculation of the Italian tax credit, generating a double advantage.
A generic practical scenario illustrates the mechanism: a cross-border worker with a certain amount of gross Swiss income pays a portion into the third pillar. Their Swiss taxable income consequently decreases, with a lower withholding tax in Switzerland. When they declare their income in Italy (reduced by the amount paid into the 3a), the Italian tax credit is calculated on a lower net income, resulting in a lower final taxation. The effect is a 'reserve' that grows over time.
### Returns and Wealth Accumulation
The returns generated by the third pillar (interest, capital gains from investments, dividends from securities) are exempt from Swiss tax until the time of withdrawal. This means that the money paid into the third pillar 'works' in a favorable regime, accumulating without fiscal erosion each year. For a cross-border worker who pays regularly from the first year of work until retirement (40+ years of career), the compound effect can be significant. Switzerland does not apply any tax on the internal growth of the 3a fund; Italy, on the other hand, does not tax the internal returns as long as the 3a remains tied up.
### Refunds: Recovering Past Taxes
Cross-border workers who have worked in Switzerland in the years prior to 2024 (effective date of the New Agreement) and have paid Swiss or Italian taxes on partially double-taxed income can apply for a refund with the competent Italian tax administration (Agenzia delle Entrate). The refund is a partial or total return of the taxes paid in excess. Even if the third pillar was not yet popular among cross-border workers at the time, some who had independently subscribed to it can benefit from refunds calculated retroactively based on the new legislation, provided that the request is submitted within the prescription terms established by the legislation.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to activate the third pillar: step-by-step procedure
### Step 1: Choose a Swiss bank or insurance company
The third pillar does not have a 'unique' counterpart in Switzerland. Commercial banks (UBS, Credit Suisse, Raiffeisen, Postfinance) and insurance companies (Allianz Switzerland, AXA, Zurich) offer 3a accounts and policies with different features. Bank 3a accounts (called 'pension account') have lower fees but returns linked to current interest rates. 3a insurance policies include disability or death protection but with slightly higher costs. Italian cross-border workers can choose freely, although most prefer Swiss banks located near Ticino border crossings (Brogeda, Chiasso, etc.) for convenience.
### Step 2: Prepare the documentation
To open a 3a account/policy, you need: - Valid ID (Italian passport or ID card) - Residence certificate in Italy (issued by the municipality of residence) - Swiss work permit G or B (authenticated copy) - Proof of Swiss income (recent pay slip, employer certificate, or withholding tax declaration)
Many Swiss banks also require a declaration of non-Swiss citizenship and a FATCA (Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act) self-certification for anti-money laundering compliance. For cross-border workers, the process is simplified: the above documents and a verifiable residence in Italy are sufficient.
### Step 3: Define the contribution plan
Once the 3a account is opened, the cross-border worker chooses the annual amount to contribute. In Switzerland, the maximum 3a contribution limit is set by federal law and varies depending on the worker's situation (employee, self-employed, etc.). For a cross-border employee in Switzerland, the rule is: contribute up to the legally set limit, deduct from the taxable income, and the returns grow undisturbed.
Contributions can be: - Weekly or monthly via automatic debit from the Swiss current account - Annual by December 31 - Occasional (provided the legal maximum limit is not exceeded)
Consult the Swiss bank at the time of opening to verify the current limit in your canton and your personal situation.
### Step 4: Deduct from the Swiss tax return
Each year, the cross-border worker receives an updated statement and a deduction certificate from their 3a institution. These documents must be attached to the Swiss withholding tax return (in Ticino, to the Tax Office of the Cantonal Tax Administration). The deduction directly reduces the withholding tax. If the cross-border worker has already made excessive payments during the year, the withholding tax refund covers the reduction of the taxable income, producing a refund check.
### Italian declaration and CE box
In Italy, the cross-border worker declares the gross Swiss income in the 730 model (foreign income section). The third pillar is not directly deducted from the Italian income (because it is a Swiss contribution), but its 'tax trace' appears in the calculation of the Swiss taxable base, and therefore in the Italian tax credit (CE box). Many cross-border workers entrust this part to an accountant experienced in cross-border tax law, as the interaction rules are complex.
### Critical deadlines
- December 31: Last day for contributions to the 3a account/policy of the current year (for deduction in the fiscal year). - March-April: Submission of the Swiss withholding tax return (cantonal). - May-June: Submission of the 730 model in Italy with foreign income and calculated tax credit. - June-July: Publication of data in Switzerland; possible withholding tax adjustments.
### Useful tools
To plan contributions and calculate the net after 3a deductibility, use the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) for cross-border workers. Also consult the guide on the [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) for in-depth information on types of plans and investment strategies. For questions about the Italian 730 declaration and CE box, see the [guide to income tax declaration](nav:tax-return) for cross-border workers.
Ready to start? Contact a Swiss bank that serves cross-border workers, gather your documents, and open a 3a account this year. Each year of difference represents lost years of returns. Your Swiss pension future starts today.

item.title: Varese train blocked in Milan bypass: inconveniences at S5
item.description: Approximately 400 passengers evacuated on 3 September from the Milan passerby. The S5, a crucial line for Ticino commuters to Milan and the hinterland, diverted to an alternative route.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Train Varese-Milano stopped on September 3 at 10 am at Lancetti station; 400 passengers evacuated - Cause: Cut electrical cable during works on the railway tunnel - S5 Varese-Milano-Treviglio (most used line by Varese commuters) diverted to alternative route - Disruptions on all 5 suburban lines: S1, S2, S3, S4, S5
## Key facts - **What**: Train Varese-Milano blocked in the tunnel after electrical cable cut - When: September 3, 2026, around 10 am - Where: Milano Lancetti station, underground railway tunnel - Who: ~400 passengers evacuated; fire brigade, railway police, 118 on site - Estimated duration: About an hour to restore circulation - Affected lines: S1, S2, S3, S4, S5 all suspended or diverted
Around four hundred people were evacuated on Wednesday, September 3, from a train that had departed from Varese and was heading to Milano, which got stuck at the Lancetti station of the railway tunnel. The event immediately caused chaos on all suburban lines, severely affecting cross-border commuters who daily use this crucial route to Milano and the Lombard hinterland.
The train stopped around 10 am. Firefighters from the Milano Command, railway police, local police, and 118 personnel immediately intervened. With the support of civil protection, passengers were assisted and subsequently evacuated from the area. No injuries were reported by the authorities.
### Electrical cable cut during tunnel works
According to reconstructions, the failure was caused by the cutting of an electrical cable during the ongoing renovation works on the tunnel roof. An inspection confirmed the fall of debris at the tunnel entrance, a direct consequence of the works in the critical area. Operations to restore circulation were estimated to take about an hour from the event.
The blockage had repercussions on the entire railway tunnel, the underground axis that crosses Milano and on which the lines connecting the capital with Varesotto, Brianza, and Lodigiano transit daily — the same areas frequented by thousands of Ticino cross-border workers who work in Lombard offices and industries. Already at 8:57 am, before the evacuation, Trenord had reported on its website a "circulation with serious criticalities" caused by the technical inconvenience. The company announced the need to completely reprogram the service, with cancellations and route variations. Check the available lines to verify the impacts on your daily travels. ### The S5: the most critical line for Varese and Ticino border workers
The most serious situation concerns the S5 Varese-Milano Passante-Treviglio line, indicated by the source as "the most used line by commuters in the province of Varese". This connection is essential not only for the residents of Varese, but also represents an essential artery for Ticino border workers who travel from Lugano, Mendrisio, Chiasso and other municipalities of the canton to work in Milan, Varese, the Malpensa area and Brianza. The suspension and subsequent diversion directly affected this broad swath of cross-border workers.
According to the rescheduling communicated by Trenord at 11.20, the S5 was routed on an alternative route, avoiding the passerby. This resulted in significant lengthenations of travel times compared to normal routes. Those who normally drive to Varese, Busto Arsizio or Malpensa to catch the train had to find alternative solutions at the last moment, with an immediate impact on work start times.
### Waterfall damage: other lines compromised
The rescheduling on 3 September also affected: - S1 Saronno-Milano Passante-Lodi, S12 and S13: fully suspended until further notice - **S2 Seveso-Milano Passante-Milano Rogoredo**: limited service only between Seveso and Milano Bovisa, skipping the passante - S3 Saronno-Milano Bovisa-Milano Cadorna and S4 Camnago-Milano Bovisa-Milano Cadorna: affected by
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Real-time monitoring: tools and channels for commuters
Trenord has invited travelers to check the status of trains via the official Trenord app and the "Real time | Lines and schedules" section of the trenord.it website. For those who commute daily from Ticino to Lombardy, it is essential to consult these channels 15-20 minutes before the scheduled departure, as disruptions can cause cascading delays even on lines not directly affected by the block.
For cross-border commuters using the S5 or other passante lines, the practical advice is to: - Check the Trenord app at least 15 minutes before leaving home or the station - Follow Trenord announcements on social media (Twitter, Facebook, Instagram) for real-time updates - Call Trenord customer service to confirm the availability of alternative trains and estimated times - Allow extra time (at least 30-45 minutes) in case of scheduled diversions
### Rescheduling: what has been canceled and what has been modified
At 11:20 AM on September 3, Trenord had communicated the complete rescheduling: - **S1, S12, S13**: not operated until further notice - S2: restricted between Seveso and Milano Bovisa (skipping the passante) - S5: rerouted on an alternative path (travel times increase significantly, potentially by 20-40 minutes depending on the terminus)
Circulation was expected to be restored within about an hour of the event, but it is not guaranteed that the subsequent scheduling was perfect. Anyone with a trip scheduled in the following hours should verify if the service had been fully restored before going to the station.
### Context: the passante returns to operation at the beginning of September
The railway passante had returned to full operation only a few days before, after a closure for maintenance that affected the stretch between Milano Rogoredo and Milano Certosa/Milano Bovisa from August 3 to 30. This means that the system, barely restored, immediately suffered two critical failures (September 2 and 3) within forty-eight hours.
For cross-border commuters who had planned to return in September after the summer break, these disruptions represent a poor sign of fragility in the railway infrastructure that supports cross-border commuting. Anyone regularly affected by disruptions on this route should report the impact to their employer, as many companies have smart working procedures or flexible hours precisely to cover compromised transportation situations. [Check with your employer the available flexibility margins](nav:jobs) and consider documenting these episodes for future negotiations on the work mode.

item.title: Mortgage for cross-border commuters: requirements and procedure in Switzerland
item.description: Practical guide for frontier workers: how to obtain a mortgage loan in Switzerland, necessary documentation, tax at source and step-by-step procedures.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - G-licensed frontiersmen can access Swiss mortgages with strict valuations - Basic requirements: stable contract, paycheck, Italian documentation - Tax at source and AVS/LPP reduce the net income considered by banks - Procedure 4-8 weeks: documentation, evaluation, underwriting ## Key facts - * * What * *: Mortgage loan for real estate purchase from G-licensed frontiersmen - Who: Frontiermen with stable employment contract in Switzerland - Where: Canton Ticino and southern Switzerland (Grisons, Valais) - When: Total procedure 4–8 weeks from first contact - Franchise: CHF 7,500 per year (old frontiermen, regime 2024–2033), CHF 10,000 (new frontiermen from 2024) - Withholdings: 8–12% federal + cantonal source tax, AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7–18% for age group ## Lead A frontierman who works in Ticino and intends to buy a real estate property in Switzerland is facing a procedure that combines Swiss banking requirements with cross-border tax obligations. Unlike a worker resident in Switzerland, the border worker must present documentation from two different legal systems and demonstrate a solvency calculated on income subject to Swiss source tax. # ## The legal prerequisite: G permit and stable contract Swiss banks do not exclude frontier workers in principle, but apply stricter assessments. The credit institution must verify that the In calculating the mortgage, the bank considers the net income after deduction of AVS, AI, IPG and LPP, reducing the margin available for repayment. This significant withholding structure is one of the main factors that limits the borrowing capacity of the frontier compared to a resident with the same gross. ### The issue of double taxation and tax credit
Italy taxes the worldwide income of its residents. A cross-border worker residing in Italy and working in Switzerland is formally an Italian resident and therefore subject to Italian IRPEF on his global income.
The Italy-Switzerland Convention to avoid double taxation, signed on **December 9, 1976**, provides that employment income is taxed in the State where the work is performed: in this case, Switzerland. Italy grants a tax credit for taxes paid in Switzerland, applicable through the CE section of the income tax return (730 or Unico).
In practice, the cross-border worker pays withholding tax in Switzerland and then recovers part of it through the Italian tax credit during the tax return. Banks, when assessing solvency, primarily look at gross Swiss income and Swiss withholdings, not the Italian tax credit that will come later. This means that the bank requires Swiss documentation (pay slips, employer's letter) as primary proof of income currently available.
### LAMal: Swiss health insurance and solvency
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory in Switzerland. A cross-border worker residing in Italy can choose to join the Swiss system (as a supplementary insured) or remain in the Italian system. However, to demonstrate complete banking solvency, it is advisable to have active Swiss health coverage: many banks consider this a sign of integration into the territory and financial stability.
Even if LAMal is not formally included in the mortgage rate calculation (it is not a recurring debt like rent), its absence can raise doubts about the overall stability of the cross-border worker in the eyes of the credit institution. LAMal deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 per adult, depending on the coverage chosen. Although not considered in the mortgage rate, these expenses further reduce the monthly savings margin.
### Employment stability: established cross-border worker vs. new hire
Cross-border workers with established employment contracts (10+ years of continuity) generally benefit from more favorable bank assessments compared to those who have recently started. Employment stability is a positive signal that the bank considers a priority.
Conversely, a "fresh" contract (less than 1 year) may be subject to stricter assessments. The bank may require additional guarantees, more extensive documentation (e.g., references from the previous employer), or a significantly lower maximum mortgage amount. The difference is not so much in the net income (often similar between the two profiles) but in the perception of the risk of employment instability. The "new" cross-border worker will need to demonstrate with additional clarity that his employment position is stable and not subject to interruptions.
### The role of the Convention and [nav:ristorni] tax refunds
In addition to the Italian tax credit, the cross-border worker can benefit from "ristorni" — amounts refunded by Canton Ticino and some Ticino municipalities to cross-border workers who pay Swiss taxes. Ristorni are not a true tax deduction but a partial refund of the tax paid.
However, ristorni generally arrive with a delay (12–18 months after payment) and are not guaranteed year by year, so the bank DOES NOT consider them in the calculation of current repayment capacity. This triple tax structure (Swiss withholding tax + Italian IRPEF + possible Ticino refund) makes the solvency analysis complex. A Swiss bank focuses on net Swiss income; the tax credit and ristorni remain secondary advantages that the cross-border worker will have to manage independently in the overall tax planning.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### The Step-by-Step Procedure
Phase 1: Preliminary Contact and Pre-Approval The cross-border worker contacts one or more Swiss banks with branches in border areas (Canton Ticino, Grisons, Valais) and requests mortgage advice. Many institutions have specific forms for cross-border workers. During the initial consultation, the bank communicates the requirements and asks for a preliminary estimate of the desired mortgage (total amount, expected duration, percentage of own contribution).
**Phase 2: Preparation of Documentation** The cross-border worker gathers employment contract, last three pay slips (originals), letter from the employer (on company letterhead, signed by the HR manager), Italian tax return (730 or Unico) for the last two years, valid ID, G/B permit. Italian documentation often needs to be translated into German or French (depending on the canton). Official translations have a cost and take 2–3 days.
Phase 3: Bank Evaluation The bank evaluates the documentation on several fronts: - Verification of employment stability (direct contact with the Swiss employer) - Calculation of available net income (gross minus withholding tax, AVS/AI/IPG, LPP, any other debts) - Estimation of the property value through internal appraisal or external appraisals - Calculation of the monthly mortgage payment and verification of compatibility with net income (generally, the payment should not exceed 33% of the net income)
Phase 4: Loan Decision If the bank approves the mortgage, it notifies the terms: total amount, interest rate (fixed or variable), duration (usually 15–25 years), amount of the monthly payment, percentage required for own contribution (usually 20–30% of the purchase price).
Phase 5: Mortgage Signing and Mortgage Registration The cross-border worker goes to the bank and a notary to sign the mortgage contract. Simultaneously, a mortgage is registered on the property with the cantonal Land Registry. This process takes about 2–4 weeks.
### Overall Timelines - Pre-approval: 1–2 weeks - Complete evaluation: 2–4 weeks - Signing and mortgage registration: 1–2 weeks - Total: 4–8 weeks from the first contact to the mortgage activation It is advisable to start the process at least 3 months before the desired purchase completion date to avoid delays due to translations, appraisals, or additional documentation requests.
### Essential Documentation: Complete Checklist 1. Employment contract — original or certified copy with employer's stamp 2. Last 3 pay slips — originals, with "gross", "deductions", "net" clearly visible 3. Letter from the employer — on company letterhead, signed by the HR manager, confirming: job position, date of hire, annual gross salary, stability prospects 4. Tax return — model 730 or Unico for the last 2 years, with certification from the Revenue Agency (must report income from employment and any deductions) 5. ID document — valid Italian passport or driver's license 6. Work permit — copy of G or B permit 7. Bank statements — for the last 3 months, to track movements and demonstrate savings capacity 8. Asset declaration — optional, if you own properties or investments in Italy (the bank may request appraisals) 9. Residence certificate — to be requested from the Italian municipality of residence (some cantons require it)
### Tax Aspects Following Mortgage Activation Once the mortgage is activated, the cross-border worker will have deductible passive interests in Italy according to IRPEF rules. In the 730 model or Unico declaration, mortgage interests reduce the Italian taxable income, producing an additional tax benefit. Furthermore, any property appreciation (in case of future sale) will be subject to taxation both in Switzerland (real estate gain tax, according to cantonal rules) and potentially in Italy (according to capital gains rules, if the property is considered an investment asset). It is advisable to consult a tax advisor familiar with cross-border taxation before activating the mortgage and certainly before selling the property.
### Next Steps: From Calculation to Signing If you are a cross-border worker interested in evaluating your mortgage capacity, the first step is to estimate your actual net income (gross minus withholding tax, AVS, LPP). Use our [nav:calculator] calculator to simulate your pay slip and understand how much remains available for mortgage repayment. Subsequently, contact the Swiss banks operating in your work area directly: many offer free consultations without obligation and can give you a preliminary estimate of mortgage capacity based on your specific documents.

item.description: Buying a house in Switzerland from a border agent is possible. Here are requirements, banks and procedures to obtain a mortgage loan in Ticino and border regions.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Cross-border workers can buy a house in Switzerland by applying for a mortgage - Requirements: income stability, work permit, tax documentation - Procedures: consult cantonal banks, verify financial capacity
## Key facts - **What**: Mortgage for property purchase in Switzerland by cross-border workers - Where: Ticino Channel, Italian-Swiss border regions (Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano) - Who: Cross-border workers with permit G, residents in Italy - When: Continuous evaluation by cantonal banks - Requirement: Documented income stability, verified financial capacity
Today, an increasing number of Ticino cross-border workers are considering buying property in Switzerland. The proximity to the workplace, the right to a cantonal residence for the future, and access to Swiss services make this option attractive for many commuting families. However, obtaining a mortgage in Switzerland requires meeting specific criteria that banks evaluate rigorously.
For a cross-border worker, the mortgage application starts from a solid base: the income from work in Switzerland is tracked, documented, and subject to withholding tax in the country of work. This represents an advantage over those working in Italy, as the continuity and stability of income are already verifiable through Swiss pay slips. However, banks operating in Ticino and border cantons apply common standards at the federal level for access to mortgage credit, and residing in Italy is not an automatic obstacle if the work permit is current.
### The issue of documentation and financial capacity
Financial capacity is the first criterion that a bank evaluates. This means that your gross annual income, your savings, and your credit history will be analyzed to determine if you can afford the monthly mortgage payments, as well as manage the expenses associated with the property (cantonal property taxes, insurance, maintenance). Banks require complete documentation: work certificates, last three pay slips, income statements (both Italian and Swiss for previous years), bank statements, and proof of own funds for the initial payment.
A cross-border worker residing in Italy must also provide a copy of the valid work permit, as it demonstrates the legitimacy of staying in Switzerland and the continuity of the employment relationship. Although the permit is not a block, its validity reassures the bank about income stability. Initial procedures require patience but represent protection for both the bank and the borrower. Access to the mortgage for a border worker also depends on a number of economic and administrative factors that deserve a closer look. Understanding these obstacles is essential so as not to be surprised during the assessment.
### What are the most common obstacles
Banks are cautious when assessing loans to non-residents of Ticino. One of the recurring doubts concerns long-term employment stability: what happens if the frontier worker loses his job in Switzerland? Unemployment insurance covers part of the income for a limited period, but it is not enough for banks. For this reason, many institutions require a guarantee from a family member residing in Switzerland or additional insurance coverage from the borrower.
A second critical aspect is the tax issue and the [ristorni](nav:ristorni). A border worker who buys a house in Switzerland will have to face two tax systems: the Swiss one (cantonal and municipal) and the Italian one. The income tax at source is only withheld in Switzerland, but the tax refunds — annual refunds according to the agreements between Italy and Switzerland — depend on the Italian tax return (EC framework of 730). This double system does not involve double taxation thanks to the Italian-Swiss convention, but the documentation required by banks to verify the tax transparency of the applicant is often more complex for a border crossing.
A third point is the evaluation of the
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). The concrete path to a mortgage involves a series of ordered steps that should be approached calmly and with planning.

### Step-by-step: from consultation to approval

**1. Initial documentation collection**
Before submitting the application, gather all the necessary material: the last three Swiss pay slips, income tax returns (IT and CH) for the past three years, bank statements for the last 3-6 months, a copy of a valid work permit, identity document, and a copy of the [health insurance policy](nav:health) (LAMal, if already subscribed in Switzerland). If you are married or cohabiting, obtain the same documentation for your spouse/partner.

2. Pre-consultation with the bank
Contact the bank for a preliminary consultation (often free). During this meeting, the bank estimates your financing capacity based on a hypothetical mortgage scenario. It is not binding, but it gives you a realistic idea of how much you can request.

3. Property search and evaluation
Once you know your maximum budget, you can start looking for properties. When you find the house, have its value estimated by an independent appraiser (or ask the bank for an estimate), and verify the cadastral conditions and any existing mortgages or encumbrances with the cantonal land registry.

4. Mortgage application submission
With the documents and the identified property, submit the mortgage application to the bank. The bank will initiate a formal credit evaluation, which includes: analysis of your income tax return, verification of employment stability, property appraisal, and search for any pre-existing mortgage burdens. The timeframe is variable, but typically 4-6 weeks.

5. Approval and signing
If approved, you will receive an official mortgage offer with the rates, duration, installments, and all clauses. You will have time to evaluate and, if accepted, proceed to the contractual signing in front of a notary. The notary formalizes the mortgage on the property.

### Practical tools for comparing offers
Not all banks offer the same rates or conditions. Use a [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate monthly installments based on the amount, duration, and interest rate. Request quotes from 2-3 different banks: the total cost of a mortgage (rate + mandatory insurance + fees) varies significantly.

Finally, remember that the own funds required by banks (your initial contribution) typically range from 10% to 20% of the estimated property value. If you have saved less, you can negotiate with the bank or ask a family member for a guarantee. This final step is crucial: do not rush to sign if you are not fully convinced of the offered conditions.

item.title: Tax deductions for border workers 2026
item.description: Deductions and tax credits for those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy: deductibles €7,500-€10,000, EC framework, tax return.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New border agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Excess €7,500 old frontier workers, €10,000 new - Source tax paid in Switzerland, credit in Italy - Declaration via EC framework of the model 730
## Key facts - **What**: New agreement on border taxation - When: 1 January 2024 (vigor) - Where: Italy-Switzerland Frontier, Canton of Ticino - Who: Frontier workers with G permit - Deductible: €7,500 (old), €10,000 (new from 17/7/2023) - Tax: Withholding tax in Switzerland, credit via CE framework
The Ticino border worker who works in Switzerland and resides in Italy today finds himself in a scenario well defined by the new legislation. From January 1, 2024, the New Frontier Agreement entered into force, signed on December 23, 2020, which outlines the definitive taxation rules for those who cross the border daily for work reasons.
## # New franchises
The main novelty concerns deductibles — that is, the income thresholds exempt from the Italian tax burden. For frontier workers who were already frontier workers before 17 July 2023 (the "old frontier workers"), the exemption is €7,500 per year under the transitional regime that lasts until 2033. For those who became border workers after that date, the deductible rises to €10,000. This means that the first tier of annual gross income, up to that threshold, is not taxed in Italy.
### How source tax works
The basic mechanism is simple but crucial: ### The declaration in Italy: the CE form
Every year, the cross-border worker who works in Switzerland must file the Italian income tax return. In the 730 form (or in the Redditi PF form if preferred), they must complete the CE form to report income earned abroad and taxes already paid.
The CE form is the tool with which the cross-border worker communicates to the Italian Revenue Agency: - The gross income received in Switzerland (from Swiss documentation) - The withholding taxes in Switzerland (federal/cantonal tax, AVS, AI, IPG, LAINF, solidarity contribution) - The request for tax credit based on what has been paid abroad
The Italian Revenue Agency then calculates whether the cross-border worker must pay additional tax in Italy (when the income exceeds the exemption and the tax credit does not fully cover the Italian tax according to the IRPEF rates: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000), or whether they will receive a refund (when the credit is higher than the Italian tax due based on the reduced amount by the exemption).
### Old vs. new cross-border workers: practical implications
The distinction of date (July 17, 2023) creates two parallel regimes until 2033. A cross-border worker who started working in Switzerland before that date enjoys an exemption of €7,500 in the transitional regime. Those who started after benefit immediately from an exemption of €10,000. This means that, with the same gross income in Switzerland, the new cross-border worker has a wider tax exemption in Italy, and therefore potentially lower Italian tax burden.
In the transitional regime that will last until 2033, the situation remains separate for the two categories of cross-border workers. It is not yet defined how the legislation will evolve beyond 2033 — the exemptions could align, increase, or remain differentiated.
### Pension and insurance system
The cross-border worker pays contributions in Switzerland for AVS (mandatory pension), LPP (second pillar), and LAMal insurance (health, with the right to choose and adult deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 depending on the chosen policy). While in Italy, they remain registered as a foreign resident for INPS purposes. This creates an administrative overlap that the new agreement seeks to manage clearly, specifying which contributions to pay in which country and how to consider them in the declaration.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Step-by-step declaration procedure
The tax declaration for cross-border workers follows a well-defined procedure that begins many months before the deadline:
**Step 1: Gather Swiss documentation** From the Swiss employer, the cross-border worker receives at the end of the year (usually by January) the withholding certificate (tax slip). This document indicates all taxes and contributions paid in Switzerland: federal withholding tax, cantonal tax, AVS, AI, IPG, LAINF, and solidarity contribution if applicable. This slip is essential to complete the CE form.
Step 2: Fill out the Italian declaration In Italy, the cross-border worker submits the 730 form (through a tax substitute or independently online on the Agenzia delle Entrate website). In the CE form, they report the gross foreign income (from Swiss documentation) and the taxes paid abroad, then request the tax credit. The Agenzia delle Entrate provides specific instructions for the CE form on its official website.
Step 3: Application of the exemption and tax calculation The Agenzia delle Entrate subtracts the due exemption (€7,500 if cross-border before 17/7/2023, €10,000 if after) from the taxable base. It calculates the Italian tax on this reduced base according to the IRPEF rates and applies the Swiss tax credit. If the credit exceeds the Italian tax, the cross-border worker is entitled to a refund.
Step 4: Respect deadlines The deadline for submitting the 730 is usually in May of the following year (with extensions to November if through CAF or accountant). Modifications and clarifications can be made by March 31 of the following year through an additional declaration.
### Essential documents to keep
- Swiss withholding certificate (employer's tax slip): key document - Bank statements: to justify cross-border income and payments - G permit: proof of cross-border status and employment relationship - Italian residence certificate: issued by the municipality of residence - Previous tax declarations: useful for consistency checks by the Agenzia delle Entrate - Communications from the Agenzia delle Entrate: any notes, corrections, or requests for clarification
### When to seek specialized help
Not all accountants have specific experience with the cross-border regime and the CE form of the double taxation convention. It is advisable to turn to an intermediary who knows the CH-IT system well, or to contact the Agenzia delle Entrate directly through the official website or regional toll-free numbers. An error in completing the CE form can lead to enforcement notices or denied refunds, so it is worth verifying the correctness of the procedure.
[Use the cross-border paycheck calculator to estimate your net income](nav:calculator) based on gross Swiss income and expected withholdings. This will help you predict the net income to declare in Italy.

item.title: Cross-border workers: 730 tax return and tax credit
item.description: Practical guide to the 730 declaration for border workers 2026: how to obtain the tax credit, avoid double taxation, new deductibles from the New Agreement.
item.content:encoded:
## In short

 - From 1 January 2024, the New Border Agreement will change taxation between Italy and Switzerland.
 - Withholding tax ONLY in Switzerland; Italy recognizes a tax credit in the EC form 730.
 - Exemption of €7,500 (old cross-border workers) or €10,000 (new cross-border workers), transitional regime until 2033

 ## Key Facts

 - **What**: Cross-border income tax return with tax credit in the CE section of Form 730
 - When: From 1 January 2024 (New Cross-Border Agreement)
 - Where: Italian Revenue Agency, for permit G
 - Who: Cross-border workers residing in Italy, employed in Switzerland
 - Exempt amount: €7,500 (already cross-border workers before 17/7/2023) or €10,000 (new)
 - IRPEF rate: 23% (up to €28,000), 35% (€28,001–€50,000), 43% (over €50,000)
 - Swiss withholding tax: 5.3% (AVS/AI/IPG) + contributions, paid in Switzerland

 ### Cross-border taxation: the New Agreement changes the rules

 The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and effective January 1, 2024, represents a turning point in the tax management of those living in Italy and working in Switzerland. The double taxation agreement between Italy and Switzerland, signed on December 9, 1976, remains the basic legal framework, but the new agreement introduces more transparent procedures and specific benefits for cross-border workers.

 The main innovation: the withholding tax on earned income is withheld exclusively in Switzerland. Italy does not apply a second tax, but ### The 730 declaration: forms and procedures

 Form 730 is mandatory for cross-border workers who wish to obtain the tax credit and, if applicable, the refund. The declaration informs the Revenue Agency of the composition of their Swiss income and the tax already paid.

 In the 730 form, cross-border workers report: gross income earned in Switzerland; the amount of withholding tax paid (AVS/AI/IPG, mandatory Swiss contributions); in the CE section, the credit for foreign taxes; and any other deductions if resident in Italy for IRPEF purposes.

 Upon receipt of the declaration, the Revenue Agency calculates the gross Italian tax on the declared income. After deducting the exemption for cross-border workers (€7,500 or €10,000), it applies the IRPEF rates: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, and 43% above €50,000. It then subtracts the foreign tax credit. If the credit exceeds the Italian tax, the cross-border worker receives a refund. If the Italian tax exceeds the credit, he or she pays the difference.

 ### Documents to be collected from the Swiss employer

 Before completing the 730 form, cross-border workers must gather documentation from Switzerland. This includes: the salary certificate (Lohnausweis / Certificat de salaire) from their employer; the official declaration of withholding tax paid (amount and period); details of mandatory contributions withheld (AVS/AI/EO, LAINF, LPP if applicable); and any other relevant amounts.

 Most ### Step-by-step procedure: from data collection to refund
Step 1: Collect Swiss documentation (by February) — Request the Lohnausweis (salary certificate), the amount of withholding tax paid, and details of contributions (AVS/AI/IPG) from the Swiss employer. Keep pay slips and bank communications.
Step 2: Calculate taxable income (March) — Check if the allowance (€7,500 or €10,000) reduces the gross Swiss income. Calculate the taxable income net of the allowance: this is the income subject to Italian IRPEF.
Step 3: Prepare the 730 form (April, by the 30th) — Fill out the 730 with the income, the allowance, the amount of Swiss withholding tax. In the CE section, enter the foreign tax credit. Convert Swiss amounts to EUR at the exchange rate of the Agenzia delle Entrate (usually the exchange rate of December 31 of the previous year).
Step 4: Submit the declaration (by April 30) — Transmit the 730 online on the Agenzia Entrate website, or through a CAF, accountant, or authorized intermediary.
Step 5: Wait for the calculation (May-August) — The Agency processes the declaration and communicates the outcome: refund or amount due. The refund, if due, is usually credited within four months of submission.
### Entities and references: where to get information
**Agenzia delle Entrate**: official website for 730 forms, instructions, and declaration outcome consultation. Public openings in local offices.
INPS: consultable to verify any mandatory contributions paid in Italy (if the cross-border worker has mixed work periods or parallel self-employment activity in Italy).
CAF/Accountants: provide support in filling out the 730 and transmitting it. Many offer specific consultations for cross-border workers.
### Deadlines 2026: what not to miss
- January 2026: receive the Lohnausweis for 2025 from the Swiss employer - April 2026 (by the 30th): deadline for submitting the 730 for 2025 - May-August 2026: the Agency processes and communicates the outcome
Use our [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate different salary scenarios and see the immediate impact of the allowance and tax credit. Our [guide to income tax returns](nav:tax-return) provides field-by-field instructions for the 730. For in-depth information on refunds and deadlines, consult the [Refunds for cross-border workers](nav:ristorni) section.

item.description: New Frontier Agreement from 2024: how to recover taxes with 730. Exemption €7,500 (old) vs €10,000 (new). Explained returns and tax credit.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024: the tax system changes - The tax credit in 730 offsets the source tax paid in Switzerland - Exemption €7,500 (old cross-border commuters) vs €10,000 (new) from 2024 - Refunds: the mechanism to recover taxes paid in excess
## Key facts - **What**: New Border Agreement redefines double taxation CH-IT - When: Effective January 1, 2024 (signed December 23, 2020) - Where: Frontier between Switzerland and Italy - Who: Italian Government (Law 83/2023) and Switzerland - Exemption amount: €7,500 (old) vs €10,000 (new) - Income tax rate: 23% up to €28,000; 35% €28,001- €50,000; 43% over €50,000
On 1 January 2024, the New Frontier Agreement entered into force, signed between Italy and Switzerland on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023. This agreement completely redefines how taxation works for those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy.
For frontier workers, the tax system is divided into two phases: first Switzerland withholds the tax at source directly from the paycheck (calculated on AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% plus any cantonal contributions), then Italy allows a tax credit through the EC framework of the tax return (730). This mechanism allows Italy to avoid double taxation according to the Italian-Swiss Convention signed on 9 December 1976.
### Transitional regime and ## Refunds and tax credits: the practical mechanism
Refunds are the heart of the system for the frontaliers. When a frontaliere pays the withholding tax in Switzerland, it is calculated on federal and cantonal rates that together can exceed the actual Italian tax burden. The difference between what is paid in Switzerland and what is due in Italy is refunded: these are the refunds.
### The CE form 730
To apply for a refund (or to check if Switzerland still has to pay it), the procedure goes through the Italian form 730. In the model, the CE form accommodates information on income earned in Switzerland, taxes paid to the Swiss tax authority (withholding tax), and tax credits claimed. The Italian Tax Authority (and upstream the MEF for bilateral agreements) cross-references the data with the Swiss tax authority. If a balance in favor of the frontaliere emerges, a refund is generated. If, on the other hand, a debt to Italy emerges, the frontaliere will have to pay the balance.
The CE form has been designed to prevent double taxation on foreign income. The Italo-Swiss Convention of December 9, 1976, establishes that the right to tax belongs to the State in which the income is produced. In this case, Switzerland taxes the employment income (withholding tax), and Italy grants an equivalent tax credit to compensate.
### Scenario: how it works in practice
Imagine a frontaliere (old category, so with an exemption of €7,500) who earns €40,000 annually gross in Switzerland. In Switzerland, he pays a withholding tax that varies depending on the canton of residence (fundamental for taxation). For simplicity, let's assume CHF 4,500 annually in withholding taxes (this is an illustrative example; the actual figure varies from canton to canton based on the combined federal and cantonal rates).
In Italy, the income of €40,000 minus the exemption of €7,500 = €32,500 taxable. With a rate of 35% (falls within the range €28,001–€50,000), he should pay approximately €11,375 in IRPEF. However, the currency exchange rate CHF-EUR (applied at the annual average rate) and the Swiss tax credit significantly reduce the debt. Often, a refund in favor of the frontaliere emerges.
### Old vs new frontaliers: the advantage accumulates over time
The difference between the exemption of €7,500 and the franchise of €10,000 is substantial. Over 33 years of transitional regime (until 2033 for old frontaliers), a new frontaliere recovers €2,500 annually in lower taxes = €82,500 in total over the period. This advantage is acquired right from the start at the time of registration in the frontaliers registry. Old frontaliers, on the other hand, will see the exemption of €7,500 expire in 2033; after that, the ordinary regime without special exemptions will apply. This expiration represents an important point of discontinuity for those who have been frontaliers for years.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## How to Apply: Step-by-Step Procedure
### Step 1: Gather the Documentation
For the 730 with the CE form, you need to collect a series of essential documents. First, the work certificate from Switzerland: it must contain the gross income earned and the total amount of taxes paid. Second, the pay stubs from February to December that document the withholding tax every month. Third, the declaration of tax residence in Italy, with the name of the municipality of residence. Finally, the Italian tax code and the number of the frontaliere permit (category G or B according to current regulations). If you have only one source of income (work in Switzerland), it is sufficient; if you also have Italian incomes (rental of a property, for example), you will need to document them separately.
### Step 2: Complete the CE Form
The CE form is dedicated exclusively to foreign income taxed abroad. In this section of the 730, you will need to enter the name of the foreign state (Switzerland), the type of income (Employment), and the gross amount of foreign income converted to EUR (convert from CHF at the average annual rate). Then declare the taxes paid in Switzerland (monthly withholding tax documented by the pay stubs), and the tax credit claimed based on the double taxation agreement. If the frontaliere also has Italian incomes (e.g., rental of a property), these must be declared separately in the real estate income section (section B of the 730), not in the CE form.
It is essential to complete this form accurately, as it is the point of intersection between the Italian tax authorities and the Swiss tax authorities. The Italian tax authorities will communicate the data to SECO (Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) to verify the correct declaration of the withholding tax. Errors or omissions here could delay the refund by weeks or months.
### Step 3: Deadline and Submission
The 730 must be submitted by October 31 of the year following the tax year (e.g., the 730 for 2024 by October 31, 2025). Frontaliers can choose from three submission methods: online via Agenzia delle Entrate using SPID or CIE credentials, through a certified CAF (Fiscal Assistance Center), or with the support of a licensed tax advisor. If you choose the CAF or the tax advisor, they will handle the electronic transmission. If you submit online on your own, remember to keep the transmission receipt for your records.
Use the [frontaliere salary calculator](nav:calculator) on our website to estimate your net pay and the expected Italian tax burden. You can check how much tax you will pay in Switzerland and whether a refund is likely to emerge. For more information on the tax credit, consult our guide to the tax credit for frontaliers. If you are looking for specific details on when refunds arrive, read [Frontaliere Refunds: When They Arrive and How to Calculate Them](nav:ristorni).
Filling out the 730 is not complicated, but it requires attention to detail: the CHF-EUR exchange rate, the correct documentation of the withholding tax, and the correct entry of data in the CE form. If you are a frontaliere for the first time, consider the support of a CAF to avoid errors that could delay the refund. Use the [calculator](nav:calculator) for an initial accurate estimate of your Swiss net and discover how much tax you may recover through refunds.

## In brief - Train strike from 7 to 8 September - 24 hours stop for commuters - Guaranteed time slots and replacement buses for Malpensa - Impact on Ticino municipalities: Lugano, Bellinzona, Chiasso
## Key facts - **What**: Train strike - When: From 7 to 8 September - Where: Italy - Who: Cub Trasporti and Sgb - Amount: 24 hours stop
The national protest proclaimed by Cub Trasporti and Sgb will involve the personnel of the Fs Group, Trenitalia and Trenord. Guaranteed time slots and replacement buses are planned for the connection with Malpensa.
A bitter start of the week for travelers and the many commuters who use the railway network daily. A new national protest risks paralyzing traffic on the tracks starting from the evening of Monday 7 September, continuing throughout Tuesday 8 September.
